Package hu.bme.mit.theta.frontend.transformation.model.types.complex.compound

Class ByteUnionSlice

java.lang.Object
hu.bme.mit.theta.frontend.transformation.model.types.complex.compound.ByteUnionSlice
public final class ByteUnionSlice extends Object
Read and write a union member that is laid out as consecutive one-byte cells rather than sharing one packed word (see CStruct#unionCellWidth). This is AD7's intractable half: a union with an array member -- or one too wide for a word, up to the 4 KB page tables in intel-tdx-module -- has no single cell for a sibling member to slice, so instead each member is the little-endian recombination of the one-byte cells at its own byte offset: Concat(cell[n-1],...,cell[0]) under bitvector, sum cell[j] * 256^j under integer. Both encodings work because the recombination is always by constant powers of 256, never a variable shift -- unlike a bit-sliced word, which would need 2^(8*i) for a variable byte index and so only works under bitvector.

Metadata keys mirror BitfieldSlice's: stamped on the value a read produces, so that an assignment through it can find what to write back to. BASE/OFFSET/ WIDTH mark a resolved (possibly multi-byte) member value. ARRAY_BASE/ARRAY_OFFSET/ARRAY_ELEMENT_BYTES mark an array-typed member accessed without its subscript yet, so that the next [i] can compute byteOff + i*elementSize before resolving to a member value in turn.

  • Method Details

    • read

      public static Expr<?> read(List<Expr<?>> cellsLsbFirst, boolean signed)
      The value of an n-byte little-endian member from its one-byte cells, cellsLsbFirst.get(0) being the lowest address (the least-significant byte) -- exactly how u.dwords[i] sits at bytes [i*4, i*4+4) with byte i*4 holding the low 8 bits. A signed read reinterprets the top bit of the whole 8*n-bit member; unsigned needs nothing extra, since every cell is already non-negative.

    • toBytes

      public static List<Expr<?>> toBytes(Expr<?> value, int n)
      Splits value -- already cast to the member's own 8*n-bit-wide type -- into its n one-byte cells, [0] being the lowest address (the least-significant byte). No read-modify-write is needed here: a whole-byte member overwrites every cell it touches outright, unlike a bitfield sharing a cell with a neighbour.
